paras: The Meansville camp meeting shooting was an exchange of gunfire between white marshals and Black men at a Black camp meeting at Meansville, Georgia, south of Zebulon, reported in a dispatch dated August 23, 1905. One Black man was killed and three others were jailed, among them an Atlanta man charged with selling whisky. The only coverage found is a brief wire item reprinted in two Florida papers.

According to the dispatch from Zebulon, a "riot" broke out at a "negro camp meeting" at Meansville, which one paper placed six miles and the other eight miles south of Zebulon. "Near 100 shots" were fired between "the white marshals and negro gamblers and liquor vendors." When it ended, one Black man was dead; the dispatch went on to mention "another," but the words describing that man's condition are lost in the printed text of both papers. The dispatch does not name the dead man or say who fired the shot that killed him.

The Gainesville Daily Sun reported that three others were in jail. One of them, Jim Williams, was described as being from Atlanta and was charged with selling whisky. No report of an inquest, of charges against the marshals or of a trial appears in the coverage.

The Gainesville Daily Sun printed the dispatch on August 24 and the Ocala Banner on August 25, both under the headline "Negro Killed at Camp Meeting." Neither paper added comment, and both carried the dispatch's description of the Black participants as "gamblers and liquor vendors" and of the clash as a "riot." The Ocala Banner's version omitted the line about the three men in jail.
No Black-press account of the shooting was found, so the story survives only in these two white papers' reprints of the wire item.

accounts.label: Wire dispatch from Zebulon
accounts.gist: A riot at a negro camp meeting at Meansville left one Black man dead after near 100 shots between white marshals and Black gamblers and liquor vendors; three were jailed, one for selling whisky.

framing.detail: Both Florida papers ran the dispatch under 'Negro Killed at Camp Meeting' without comment, calling the Black participants 'gamblers and liquor vendors' and the clash a 'riot'.
